title: Applying justification, learning and roles to a scenario
blurb: Decide whether a scenario action applies business justification, learning from experience or roles and relationships, and judge how well.
question: At Calderbrook Borough Council the project manager calls two other councils that already run online permit services before writing the project brief. Which principle is being applied, and why?

teach.body: Each principle question in the Practitioner paper describes something a person did and asks which principle it applies, or how well. For this trio, ask what the action is FOR. Is it testing whether the project is still worth doing? Is it seeking, recording or using lessons? Is it about who does what and how people relate? The answer that wins names the right principle AND the reason that fits these facts.

rows.label: When
values: Start, every stage end, each change
Set up in SU, revisited later

rows.label: Sounds like
values: Benefits still outweigh cost and risk

teach.caption: Section numbers for the open book: 2.1 justification, 2.2 learning, 2.3 roles, responsibilities and relationships.

teach.body: Formally: there must be a justifiable reason to start, and it must stay valid and be revalidated throughout; if it lapses, the project should stop. In plain English: keep asking whether the benefits still outweigh the costs and risks. Compulsory projects still justify the CHOSEN option as best value. Every party, suppliers included, needs its own balance of benefits, costs and risks. A request for change is weighed the same way.

children.label: Applied well
children.sub: Updated benefits weighed against remaining cost and risk

children.label: Applied poorly
children.sub: Sunk cost is not a reason to continue

children.label: Applied poorly
children.sub: It must be revalidated through the life

teach.caption: If the updated case no longer stacks up, the right move is to stop, not to carry on hopefully.

teach.body: Formally: the team actively seeks, records and implements lessons from earlier projects and as the project goes on, and shares them for others. In plain English: look back before you start, keep learning while you work, pass it on at the end. If the work is a first for the business, looking outside, to other organizations, matters even more. Learn from successes as well as mistakes.

items.label: Assess previous lessons; look outside if novel
Record in the lessons log; share insights
Review lessons; a lessons report if useful

teach.body: Formally: a defined and agreed structure of roles that engages business, user and supplier interests, and a project management team that builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders. In plain English: the right people, each knowing what is expected of them and what they can expect from others, plus deliberate effort on relationships. 'Relationships' is the PRINCE2 7 addition.

items: The council has run few projects this size, and its last app went 40% over budget without the contact centre being told.
In starting up, Hannah Okoro (PM) reviews that app's lessons and calls two councils that already run online permits: learn from experience, applied well because the work is new to Calderbrook.

Graham Pell (executive) has the outline business case compare replacement with paying £140,000 for a year more support: justification of the chosen option, even though the old system's end forces action.
Hannah sets up monthly sessions with the contact centre manager, Dev Mistry: building relationships, so the launch failure is not repeated.

teach.text: Two traps. First, 'all parties need a balance of benefits, costs and risks' is the JUSTIFICATION principle, while 'business, user and supplier interests must be represented' is the ROLES principle: both mention suppliers. Second, a compulsory or deadline-driven project still needs justification of the chosen option; 'it is forced on us' never removes the business case.

items: Justification (2.1): revalidate through the life, stop if no longer justified, every party needs its own case.
Learning (2.2): seek, record, implement and share lessons; look outside when the work is novel.
Roles (2.3): defined and agreed roles for business, user and supplier, plus relationships with stakeholders.
Pick the reason that explains THIS action; a true principle statement that fits a different action is the classic distractor.

summary: You can now tell whether a scenario action applies ensure continued business justification, learn from experience, or define roles, responsibilities and relationships. You can also judge how well it is applied by matching the action to the reason that genuinely explains it.

A.q: Calderbrook Borough Council is in the 'starting up a project' process for its online permit service, the first digital service of this kind it has built. Before assembling the project brief, the project manager arranges calls with two other councils that already run online permit services. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Learn from experience, because work that is new to the business makes lessons from other organizations more important
Learn from experience, because lessons should be shared during the project in ways that suit people's learning needs
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team should build relationships with external stakeholders
Ensure continued business justification, because each option should be compared with what similar councils spent
A.why: Reviewing similar projects at the start is learn from experience, and when the work is a 'first' for the business it is even more important to learn from others, including external organizations (2.2).

whyNot.1: Sharing insights in ways that suit different learning needs is part of the principle, but the PM is gathering lessons from outside before starting, not sharing the project's own lessons.
whyNot.2: Building relationships is part of the roles principle (2.3), but the purpose of these calls is to learn what worked elsewhere, not to build a lasting relationship.
whyNot.3: Comparing options belongs to justification (2.1), but the calls are about lessons from experience, not about the cost of the chosen option.

A.q: At Tarnside College the tender returns at the end of stage 2 show that the cheapest compliant bid would take total cost to £5.6 million against an approved £5.1 million. The executive tells the board, 'We have already spent £300,000 on design, so we must carry on', and the board authorizes stage 3 without the business case being updated. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: It applies it well, because stopping now would put the college's £4.2 million grant at risk
It applies it well, because the board is deciding at a stage end whether the project should continue
It applies it poorly, because the decision rests on money already spent, not on a revalidated case
It applies it poorly, because the senior user rather than the executive owns the business case
A.why: Justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project (2.1). Past spend is not a reason to continue; the board needed an updated business case weighing the new cost against the benefits and risks.

whyNot.0: The grant is a real factor, but it belongs in an updated business case; the executive decided without revalidating the case at all.
whyNot.1: A stage end is the right moment (manage by stages), but the decision was not based on the justification, so the principle was applied poorly.
whyNot.3: The executive owns the business case and is accountable for continued justification; the senior user specifies the benefits.

A.q: At Wenmoor Community Health, during 'starting up a project', the executive asks the head of nursing for Eastfield to act as senior user and the account manager of the patient record system supplier to act as senior supplier, so that the project board covers each main interest. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Ensure continued business justification, because every party needs a balance of benefits, costs and risks
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team should build relationships with GPs
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because business, user and supplier must all be represented
Manage by exception, because each board member is given delegated authority within agreed tolerances
A.why: All three primary stakeholder interests (business, user and supplier) must be represented in the project management team, and this is reflected in the design of the project board (2.3).

whyNot.0: Each party's own justification is part of 2.1, but the action here is choosing who holds board roles, not testing anyone's benefits and costs.
whyNot.1: Building relationships is part of 2.3, but no GP is involved in this action; it is about filling the board roles.
whyNot.3: Tolerances are delegated to the project manager by the board, not to individual board members, and the action is about representation.

B.q: On Calderbrook's online permit project, the supplier Kestrel Lane Digital works on a time-and-materials contract capped at £620,000. Its delivery director, the senior supplier, asks her finance team to review the agency's expected margin and contract risk at each stage end before she commits more staff. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the supplier interest must be represented on the board
Ensure continued business justification, because the council's business case is revalidated at each stage end
Manage by stages, because stage ends are the points at which commitments to the next stage are made
Ensure continued business justification, because a supplier needs its own justification for being involved
B.why: All parties, including suppliers, need a balance of expected benefits, costs and risks to justify their involvement (2.1). The supplier is checking its own justification, not the council's.

whyNot.0: Supplier representation is part of 2.3, but the action is a review of the agency's margin and risk, not a decision about board membership.
whyNot.1: The right principle, but the wrong reason: the council's business case is a separate matter from the supplier's own review of its margin.
whyNot.2: Stage ends are decision points for the project board; the supplier is testing its own commercial case, which is justification.

B.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the pilot wave of ten applications is complete. The project manager runs a session where the Edinburgh and Pune engineers discuss what slowed the rollback tests, records the points, and has the migration runbook changed before wave 1 starts. How well does this apply the 'learn from experience' principle, and why?
options: It applies it well, because lessons are being sought, recorded and acted on while the project is running
It applies it well, because similar earlier projects should be reviewed before a project is started
It applies it poorly, because lessons should wait for the lessons report produced at the end of each stage
It applies it poorly, because lessons are passed on to the business when the project is closed
B.why: The principle covers learning throughout the project, not just at the start and the end: the team seeks, records and implements lessons as it goes (2.2).

whyNot.1: Reviewing earlier projects at the start is part of 2.2, but this session happens mid-project, after the pilot wave.
whyNot.2: A lessons report may be produced at a stage end, but lessons can be acted on at any time; waiting would waste the insight before wave 1.
whyNot.3: Passing lessons on at closure is part of the principle, but it is not a reason to delay applying them now.

B.q: On Carrowford City Council's half marathon, the project manager sets up a monthly meeting between the race management company's race director, the police events planning officer and the council's licensing team, so that they agree how race-day decisions will be shared. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Learn from experience, because the race company's medical response was criticized at an earlier race
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team builds relationships between stakeholders
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because business, user and supplier sit on the board
Manage by exception, because decisions should be taken at the most local level that has the knowledge
B.why: The project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (2.3). The police and licensing team are stakeholders, not board members.

whyNot.0: The earlier criticism is a lesson worth using, but the meeting is about how three parties will work together, not about that lesson.
whyNot.2: Board representation is part of 2.3, but none of these people are being placed on the project board.
whyNot.3: Local decision-making is how manage by exception applies to people (3.5.1), but the meeting builds relationships rather than setting levels of authority.

C.q: In the private beta of Calderbrook's permit service, online take-up in the pilot ward is 35% against a planned 70%. Before the board decides on the final stage, the executive asks the project manager to update the business case with the new take-up forecast and show whether the benefits still justify the remaining costs and risks. Is this an appropriate application of the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the benefits should be reviewed after the project to see whether they have materialized
Yes, because the justification must stay valid and be revalidated using the latest forecasts
No, because the old system's support end makes the project compulsory, so it needs no revalidation
No, because forecasting benefits is the senior user's job, so the executive should not ask for it
C.why: The justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project (2.1). A big shortfall in take-up changes the benefits, so the case must be updated before the board commits to the next stage.

whyNot.0: Post-project benefits reviews are part of 2.1, but this check happens before the next stage decision, using forecasts, not actual results.
whyNot.2: Compulsory or deadline-driven projects still need their chosen option justified, and the justification can change as the project runs.
whyNot.3: The senior user specifies the benefits and shows they are on track, but the executive owns the business case and can rightly ask for it to be updated.

C.q: During 'starting up a project' at Wenmoor Community Health, the project manager learns that a 2021 attempt at central booking in the rural locality was abandoned after four months and that nobody recorded why. She decides not to look into it, because there are no records and the new service uses different software. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because lessons from a project that used a different system are unlikely to be relevant now
Yes, because lessons are recorded in the lessons log from the point the project starts up
No, because earlier similar work should be reviewed, and people involved can share what was learned
No, because the trust board has asked for a written record of what this project learns
C.why: Previous or similar projects should be reviewed when starting (2.2), and much valuable knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem and learned socially from people (3.5.1). Staff who took part in 2021 still hold that knowledge.

whyNot.0: The failure was about central booking and staff acceptance, which is exactly what the new service faces; the software difference does not make it irrelevant.
whyNot.1: The lessons log is started in starting up, but that is about recording new lessons, not a reason to skip earlier ones.
whyNot.3: The board's request is about recording this project's lessons; it does not explain why the 2021 experience should be sought out.

C.q: On Calderbrook's permit project, a cabinet member asks to sit on the project board. The executive agrees to add her as a fourth board member 'to represent residents' interests', with no role description, saying her duties will become clear as the project goes on. Is this an appropriate application of the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because people outside the project team, such as councillors, should be engaged
Yes, because the executive is responsible for appointing the rest of the team
No, because the board should hold no more than three people, one for each interest
No, because people need agreed roles so they know what is expected of them
C.why: Roles and responsibilities must be defined and agreed, so the right people know what is expected of them and what they can expect from others (2.3). Leaving her duties to 'become clear' breaks that.

whyNot.0: Engaging stakeholders matters, but it can be done without a board seat, and it does not justify a board role with no defined responsibilities.
whyNot.1: The executive does appoint the rest of the project management team, but that authority does not remove the need to define the role.
whyNot.2: There is no three-person limit: senior user and senior supplier roles can be held by several people.

reteach.title: Ask what the action is for
reteach.question: Strip away the names and numbers. Is the person checking value, using knowledge, or arranging people?

blocks.body: Checking whether the project is still worth it, for the business or for a supplier, is justification. Looking for, recording or using lessons, from before or during the project, is learning. Choosing who holds which role, writing what they do, or building ties between people and groups is roles, responsibilities and relationships. Decide the purpose first, then look for the option whose reason explains this action.

blocks.text: A distractor that quotes the right principle with a reason about a DIFFERENT action is still wrong. Read the reason against the facts in the stem.

explain.body: The case is made in starting up, built fully in initiation, and revalidated at every stage end and whenever a change is weighed. If it no longer holds, the board should stop the project.

test.q: At Fernhollow Foods, the sales director asks to add a seventh recipe to the launch range. The project manager's assessment sets the extra sales it might bring against the £120,000 extra cost and the new allergen risk before the board decides. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Focus on products, because the extra recipe would need its own product description
Ensure continued business justification, because a change's benefit is weighed against its cost and risk
Manage by exception, because the change might push the stage outside its cost tolerance
Ensure continued business justification, because the benefits are reviewed after the range is launched
test.why: What the project delivers must stay consistent with the evolving justification, so a request for change is judged by weighing its extra benefit against extra cost and risk (2.1).

whyNot.0: A new product would need a description, but the assessment described is about value, not about defining the product.
whyNot.2: Tolerance may matter later, but the stem describes weighing benefits against costs and risks, not a forecast breach.
whyNot.3: The right principle with the wrong reason: post-launch reviews check actual benefits, while this is a decision made in advance.

explain.body: A project driven by law, regulation or a hard deadline still has options. The business case shows that the chosen option is best value, even when doing nothing is not possible.

rows.label: Claim
values: It is forced, so no case
It is forced, so pick best value

test.q: Brennan Mutual must leave its leased data centre because the landlord will not renew the lease. During initiation the executive says that, as the exit is forced on the society, there is no point comparing hosting options in the business case. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
options: It applies it poorly, because even a forced project must justify that its chosen option is best value
It applies it poorly, because the senior user should decide which hosting option is chosen
It applies it well, because a project driven by an outside deadline has no realistic alternative
It applies it well, because the executive is the single point of accountability for the project
test.why: Compulsory projects still require justification of the chosen approach to show it represents best value for money (2.1).

whyNot.1: The executive owns the business case; the senior user specifies requirements and benefits rather than choosing the option alone.
whyNot.2: A deadline removes 'do nothing' but leaves several ways to meet it, and the chosen way must be justified.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable, but accountability does not remove the need for a justified choice of option.

explain.body: Lessons count when they change what the project does. Reading an old lessons report and then building its fixes into the controls is the principle working well.

test.q: At Tarnside College the lessons report from a small lab refurbishment said contractor progress was reported only verbally and site changes were agreed without checking the budget. The new project manager makes written contractor reports a contract term and routes every site change through the issue procedure. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Manage by exception, because changes to the budget must be escalated beyond the site team
Learn from experience, because lessons should be shared with people in ways that suit them
Learn from experience, because lessons from earlier projects are being built into this one
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the contractor's duties are being set
test.why: The project seeks lessons from previous projects and implements them (2.2): both fixes come straight from the earlier lessons report.

whyNot.0: Escalation is part of manage by exception, but the reason for these controls is the earlier lesson, not a forecast breach.
whyNot.1: Sharing lessons in suitable ways is part of 2.2, but here lessons are being applied, not shared.
whyNot.3: The contract term does set a duty, but it is there because of the lesson; the stem is about using past experience.

explain.body: Roles must be defined and agreed so people know what to expect. Relationships are built on purpose, with and between internal and external stakeholders, not left to chance.

head: Half
Looks like
rows: Agreed role descriptions; business, user, supplier on the board
Regular contact with key internal and external groups

test.q: On Fernhollow Foods' launch project, the project manager notices that the co-manufacturer and the packaging supplier have never spoken, although the trays must fit both factories' lines. She sets up a joint working group with both suppliers' technical leads. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team builds relationships between stakeholders
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because each supplier needs an agreed role description
Focus on products, because the trays must be specified so that both lines can use them
Ensure continued business justification, because each supplier needs its own business case
test.why: The project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (2.3). The working group links two suppliers who must work together.

whyNot.1: Role descriptions belong to the principle too, but the action is creating a relationship between suppliers, not defining a role.
whyNot.2: The trays do need a clear specification, but the action described is bringing two parties together.
whyNot.3: Suppliers do need their own justification, but nothing in the action tests their benefits or costs.
